summary.text: Julius Caesar was a Roman general, statesman and author who was dictator of the Roman Republic almost continuously from 49 BC until his assassination in 44 BC.
He led Roman armies through the Gallic Wars, then crossed the Rubicon against the Senate's order in 49 BC and won the civil war that followed.
Senators murdered him fearing he might make himself king, new civil wars followed, and his heir Octavian later turned the Republic into the Roman Empire.

facts.label: First Triumvirate
facts.value: Formed in 60 BC with Crassus and Pompey

facts.label: Assassinated
facts.value: Killed on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BC

facts.label: Gallic Wars
facts.value: Completed by 51 BC, greatly expanding Roman territory

items.prompt: In early 49 BC the Senate ordered Caesar to give up his command and return to Rome. He crossed the Rubicon with his army instead. What did that act begin?

options.label: A peaceful handover of his army
A new war against the Gauls
A civil war, which he won
A rebellion led by Pompey against him

items.explain: Crossing the Rubicon openly defied the Senate and began Caesar's civil war, which he won.

items.prompt: A group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius plotted against Caesar. What did they fear?

options.label: His domination of the state and a possible bid to be king
His plan to give his power back to Pompey
His string of defeats in foreign wars
His plan to shrink the Senate sharply

items.explain: They feared his power, his domination of the state, and the possibility that he might make himself king.

items.prompt: After Caesar's assassination, what became of the Republic's constitutional government?

options.label: It was restored at once with newly elected consuls
Pompey returned and rebuilt it
The Senate named another dictator for life
New civil wars began and it was never fully restored

items.explain: A new series of civil wars broke out and the constitutional government of the Republic was never fully restored.

items.prompt: After winning the civil war, Caesar carried out reforms. Which was one of them?

options.label: Settling his veterans in new overseas colonies
Cutting the size of the Senate in half
Increasing the size of the grain dole
Restoring the old republican calendar

items.explain: He settled veterans in overseas colonies, greatly increased the Senate, reduced the grain dole and replaced the republican calendar.

items.prompt: The Julii claimed their clan was divine. What was the basis for the claim?

options.label: Descent from a king of Rome who was a son of Mars
The priesthood of Jupiter held by Caesar's father
A gift of land from Tullus Hostilius
Descent from Julus, son of Aeneas, who was a son of Venus

items.explain: The family claimed descent from Julus, son of Aeneas, and since Aeneas was a son of Venus, this made the clan divine.

items.prompt: A trivia buff says Caesar was born by Caesarian section. Why does that claim fail?

options.label: Ancient sources say his mother died in childbirth
Such operations meant the mother's death, but his mother lived for decades
The operation was forbidden by law for patricians
He was born at sea, far from any surgeon

items.explain: There is no evidence for it: such operations entailed the mother's death, yet Caesar's mother lived for decades after his birth.

paragraphs.heading: Who he was
paragraphs.text: Gaius Julius Caesar, born on 12 or 13 July 100 BC, was a Roman general, statesman and writer. He ruled the Roman Republic as dictator almost without a break from 49 BC until he was killed in 44 BC. He helped create the conditions in which the Republic collapsed and the Roman Empire emerged, and for that he is counted among the most influential people in history.

paragraphs.heading: An old family
paragraphs.text: Caesar was born into the gens Julia, a patrician family that claimed descent from Julus, son of Aeneas. Since Aeneas was a son of the goddess Venus, the claim made the clan divine. For all this ancient pedigree, the family carried little political weight in the middle Republic, though its fortunes recovered in the early first century, with consuls in 91 and 90 BC. The story that Caesar was born by Caesarian section has no evidence behind it: his mother lived for decades after his birth.

paragraphs.heading: Alliance and conquest
paragraphs.text: In 60 BC Caesar joined Crassus and Pompey in the First Triumvirate, an informal alliance that controlled Roman politics for several years. Many senators opposed their grab for power, among them Cato the Younger. Caesar's victories in the Gallic Wars, finished by 51 BC, greatly enlarged Roman territory and made him one of the most powerful politicians in the Republic. Along the way he invaded Britain and built a bridge over the Rhine.

paragraphs.heading: Crossing the Rubicon
paragraphs.text: His successes and the loyalty of his veteran troops threatened to overshadow Pompey, and by 50 BC Pompey had sided with the Senate. As Caesar's command was running out, the Senate told him to give up his military command and come back to Rome. In early January 49 BC he defied that order, crossing the Rubicon and marching on Rome with an army behind him. The civil war that followed ended in his victory, and by 45 BC his power was almost unchallenged.

paragraphs.heading: Reforms in power
paragraphs.text: Once in control, Caesar pardoned many of his enemies and launched reforms and public works. He brought in the Julian calendar in place of the old lunisolar republican one. He also cut the grain dole, settled his veterans in new colonies overseas, made the Senate much larger, and gave citizenship to communities in Spain and in what is now northern Italy. In early 44 BC he was declared dictator in perpetuity.

paragraphs.heading: The Ides of March
paragraphs.text: Afraid of his power and that he could crown himself king, senators led by Brutus and Cassius killed him on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BC. New civil wars followed, and the Republic's constitutional government was never fully restored. His great-nephew and adopted heir Octavian, later called Augustus, won sole power thirteen years later. He then turned the Republic into the Roman Empire and became its first emperor.

paragraphs.heading: How we know him
paragraphs.text: Caesar wrote accounts of his own military campaigns, and much of what is known about his life comes from them. Other sources from his time are the letters and speeches of Cicero and the histories of Sallust, while later lives by Suetonius and Plutarch also matter. His name outlived him: Caesar became another word for emperor, a title used throughout the Roman Empire that lives on in Kaiser and Tsar.
